text:
A: Hiya! Oh, can you hear me okay? I'm Holly.
B: Yes, I can hear. Hello, I'm Ioana.
A: Ioana, lovely. Erm, did you manage that puzzle thing at the start? Because I sort of just guessed the last few, honestly.
B: I finished, but I don't know if it was right. It was a bit strange.
A: Weirdly stressful for something that didn't matter, yeah? So where are you calling from?
B: London. Burnt Oak, in the north-west. Near Edgware.
A: Oh nice, I'm in Birmingham, Kings Heath. My dog's asleep behind me, that's Pickle. She's a greyhound, she won't walk in the rain, so today she's basically just a tail on the settee.
B: I saw her in your photo. And the painting, I liked the painting. With the orange.
A: Oh my god, that's mine! I did that. It's not, like, good, it's kind of just cheap acrylics and vibes, you know, and it's wonky because I hung it myself. But thank you, that's made my day.
B: No, I think it has something. The colours are brave. Do you paint a lot?
A: Erm, I start a lot. There's about six half-done ones stacked behind the sofa. I'm a PhD student really, geography, so the painting is sort of procrastination with extra steps.
B: What is the PhD about?
A: So it's on old canal-side industrial spaces, the derelict warehouses and wharves round Birmingham, and how people sort of use them and reclaim them. Graffiti artists, raves, people fishing, people just sitting there having a can. I go and photograph them and interview people. Which mostly means I climb through fences and call it fieldwork.
B: That is interesting. Like the paintings of empty rooms, maybe. Places where people were, and now are not.
A: Yes! Exactly that, kind of the ghost of the use. Is that what's on your fridge? I clocked a postcard in your picture.
B: Yes, Hammershøi. Danish painter. Grey rooms, a woman with her back to you, a door open. Very quiet. I saw some at the National Gallery and I could not stop looking.
A: Oh, I love that. I'm writing that name down. Are you a big gallery person then?
B: Yes. It's the main thing I do. On my days off I go alone, National Gallery, Tate, Wellcome. I stay maybe four hours. My husband says I live there.
A: Alone is the best way, isn't it, because no one's hovering going "are we done yet". What do you do for work, sorry, if you don't mind me asking?
B: I clean at a primary school. Evening shift, after the children go. So I have the mornings for museums.
A: That's actually a really good setup, sort of. Do you like it in the school when it's empty?
B: Yes, actually. It is quiet, I listen to Radio 3. Sometimes very strange music, I don't know what it is, but I like it. And the empty classroom at night is a bit like your warehouses. The chairs on the tables.
A: Oh, that's a gorgeous image, the chairs on the tables. Can I nick that for a conference paper? I've got one in three weeks and I haven't written a single word, so honestly I need all the help going.
B: You can have it. Free.
A: Ha, perfect. Did you study art, then, or is it just a love thing?
B: I started literature, in Romania, in Iași. Romanian and French. But I left in second year, there was no money. So now I just read. Three languages, from library.
A: Three languages! I've got three novels on the go and that's my limit. What are you reading at the minute?
B: Ishiguro, The Remains of the Day. In English. It is slow, but I think it is about a man who doesn't let himself feel anything.
